While more effective than conventional language-model pre-training due to learning bidirectional representations, these masked language modeling (MLM) approaches incur a substantial compute cost because the network only learns from 15% of the tokens per example.
Training ELECTRA-Large further results in an even stronger model that outperforms ALBERT on GLUE and sets a new state-of-the-art for SQuAD 2.0.
For SQuAD, we evaluate on versions 1.1, in which models select the span of text answering a question, and 2.0, in which some questions are unanswerable by the passage.
For SQuAD, we evaluate on versions 1.1, in which models select the span of text answering a question, and 2.0, in which some questions are unanswerable by the passage.
For most experiments we pre-train on the same data as BERT, which consists of 3.3 Billion tokens from Wikipedia and BooksCorpus .

For SQuAD, we add the question-answering module from XLNet on top of ELECTRA, which is slightly more sophisticated than BERT's in that it jointly rather than independently predicts the start and end positions and has a "answerability" classifier added for SQuAD 2.0.

The results also demonstrate the strength of ELECTRA at a moderate size; our base-sized ELECTRA model substantially outperforms BERT-Base and even outperforms BERT-Large (which gets 84.0 GLUE score).
Unsurprisingly, training ELECTRA longer improves results further: ELECTRA-1.75M scores higher than previous models on the SQuAD 2.0 benchmark.

Perhaps replaced token detection, in which the model distinguishes real tokens from plausible fakes, is particularly transferable to the answerability classification of SQuAD 2.0, in which the model must distinguish answerable questions from fake unanswerable questions.

First, we find that ELECTRA is greatly benefiting from having a loss defined over all input tokens rather than just a subset: ELECTRA 15% performs much worse than ELECTRA.

We note that BERT (including our implementation) already includes a trick to help with the pre-train/fine-tune discrepancy: masked tokens are replaced with a random token 10% of the time and are kept the same 10% of the time.

We note that BERT (including our implementation) already includes a trick to help with the pre-train/fine-tune discrepancy: masked tokens are replaced with a random token 10% of the time and are kept the same 10% of the time.
However, this method suffers from the same inefficiencies as BERT because XLNet only generates 15% of the input tokens in this way.

The gains are particularly strong for small models; for example, we train a model on one GPU for 4 days that outperforms GPT (trained using 30x more compute) on the GLUE natural language understanding benchmark.

For example, we build an ELECTRA-Small model that can be trained on 1 GPU in 4 days. ELECTRA-Small outperforms a comparably small BERT model by 5 points on GLUE, and even outperforms the much larger GPT model .

However, for our Large model we pre-trained on the data used for XLNet , which extends the BERT dataset to 33B tokens by including data from ClueWeb , CommonCrawl, and Gigaword .

We train BERT-Small for 1.5M steps, so it uses the same training FLOPs as ELECTRA-Small, which was trained for 1M steps. In addition to BERT, we compare against two less resource-intensive pre-training methods based on language modeling: ELMo and GPT . We also show results for a base-sized ELECTRA model comparable to BERT-Base.

ELECTRA-Small is trained mostly to convergence, with models trained for even less time (as little as 6 hours) still achieving reasonable performance.
In particular, we train a model for 400k steps (ELECTRA-400K; roughly 1/4 the pre-training compute of RoBERTa) and one for 1.75M steps (ELECTRA-1.75M; similar compute to RoBERTa).

edges.sentence: We train BERT-Small for 1.5M steps, so it uses the same training FLOPs as ELECTRA-Small, which was trained for 1M steps.[ELECTRA requires more FLOPs per step because it consists of the generator as well as the discriminator.] In addition to BERT, we compare against two less resource-intensive pre-training methods based on language modeling: ELMo [Peters et al. 2018] and GPT [Radford et al. 2018].[GPT is similar in size to BERT-Base, but is trained for fewer steps.] We also show results for a base-sized ELECTRA model comparable to BERT-Base.
edges.title: Improving language understanding by generative pre-training
edges.authors: Alec Radford, Karthik Narasimhan, Tim Salimans, and Ilya Sutskever

edges.sentence: We evaluate on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark [Wang et al. 2019] and Stanford Question Answering (SQuAD) dataset [Rajpurkar et al. 2016].
edges.title: GLUE: A multi-task benchmark and analysis platform for natural language understanding
edges.authors: Alex Wang, Amapreet Singh, Julian Michael, Felix Hill, Omer Levy, and Samuel R Bowman

assumptions.sentence: We hypothesize that ELECTRA benefits from tied token embeddings because masked language modeling is particularly effective at learning these representations: while the discriminator only updates tokens that are present in the input or are sampled by the generator, the generator's softmax over the vocabulary densely updates all token embeddings.

assumptions.sentence: We speculate that having too strong of a generator may pose a too-challenging task for the discriminator, preventing it from learning as effectively.
assumptions.anchorText: We speculate that having too strong of a generator may pose a too-challenging task for the discriminator, preventing it from learning as effectively.

assumptions.sentence: We believe the worse accuracy is mainly due to the poor sample efficiency of reinforcement learning when working in the large action space of generating text.

assumptions.sentence: We speculate that ELECTRA is more parameter-efficient than BERT because it does not have to model the full distribution of possible tokens at each position, but we believe more analysis is needed to completely explain ELECTRA's parameter efficiency.
